blocks.title: DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES – SHAPING THE FUTURE OF GLOBAL HEALTH
blocks.content:
THE FUTURE OF GLOBAL HEALTH
The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development1 highlights that 
the spread of information and communications technology and 
global interconnectedness has great potential to accelerate human 
progress, to bridge the digital divide and to develop knowledge 
societies.
The outcome document of the high-level meeting of the 
United Nations General Assembly on the overall review of the 
implementation of the outcomes of the World Summit on 
Information Society (New York, 15–16 December 2015) highlighted 
the technology-enabled breakthroughs in government in the 
provision

summary.text: Describes how digital technologies are shaping global health, citing the 2030 Agenda and UN reviews of the World Summit on the Information Society. It argues that digital and frontier technologies can help reach WHO's triple billion targets and improve diagnosis, treatment and self-care. It notes that many countries still need support for national strategies and that digital health should be ethical, safe, equitable and interoperable.

blocks.content: Photograph of a smiling older woman with grey hair and glasses, wearing a yellow polo shirt, using a smartphone in a green case while seated at a table at home.

blocks.title: VISION
blocks.content:
VISION
The vision of the global strategy is to improve health for everyone, 
everywhere by accelerating the development and adoption of 
appropriate, accessible, affordable, scalable and sustainable person-
centric digital health solutions to prevent, detect and respond 
to epidemics and pandemics, developing infrastructure and 
applications that enable countries to use health data to promote 
health and well-being, and to achieve the health-related Sustainable 
Development Goals and the triple billion targets of WHO’s Thirteenth 
General Programme of Work, 2019–2023.
Digital health will be va

summary.text: Sets out the strategy's vision of better health for everyone through appropriate, affordable and sustainable person-centred digital health solutions, including for epidemics and pandemics. It lists the conditions under which digital health will be valued and calls for evidence on global solutions in different country contexts.

blocks.title: PURPOSE
blocks.content:
through the application of digital health technologies for consumers, 
health professionals, health care providers and industry towards 
empowering patients and achieving the vision of health for all. The 
strategy is designed to be fit for purpose and for use by all Member 
States including those with limited access to digital technologies, 
goods and services. In the context of this global strategy, digital 
health is understood to mean “the field of knowledge and practice 
associated with the development and use of digital technologies 
to improve health”. This definition encompasses eHealt

summary.text: States the strategy's purpose of strengthening health systems by applying digital technologies for patients, professionals, providers and industry, and defines digital health broadly to include eHealth and emerging fields. It stresses health data protection, interoperability and appropriate sharing of data for public benefit. It ends by saying the strategy will produce concrete actions and results between 2020 and 2025.

blocks.title: Acknowledge that institutionalization of digital health in the national health system requires a decision and commitment by countries
blocks.content:
national health system requires a decision and commitment 
by countries
The global strategy acknowledges that each country owns its digital 
health action plan built on the strategy, within its own national 
context. Along their path towards the health-related Sustainable 
Development Goals, countries will adopt digital health in a way that 
is sustainable, respects their sovereignty, and best suits their culture 
and values, national health policy, vision, goals, health and well-being 
needs, and available resources.

summary.text: States the guiding principle that each country owns its digital health action plan and will adopt digital health in line with its own context and resources.

blocks.title: Recognize that successful digital health initiatives require an integrated strategy
blocks.content:
integrated strategy
Digital technologies are an essential component and an enabler of 
sustainable health systems and universal health coverage. To realize 
their potential, digital health initiatives must be part of the wider 
health needs and the digital health ecosystem and guided by a 
robust strategy that integrates leadership, financial, organizational, 
human and technological resources and is used as the basis for 
a costed action plan which enables coordination among multiple 
stakeholders. These initiatives should be led through strong 
governance structures. The strategy should addr

summary.text: Explains that digital health initiatives need an integrated, costed strategy with strong governance, standards and architecture. It warns that poorly coordinated initiatives lead to fragmented stand-alone systems.

blocks.content:

blocks.title: Promote the appropriate use of digital technologies for health
blocks.content:
The global strategy promotes the appropriate use of digital 
technologies as digital public goods which are adaptable to different 
countries and contexts to help address key health system challenges 
to support equity in access to digital resources so that no one is 
left behind. It promotes the protection of people, populations, 
health care professionals and systems against misinformation and 
the misuse of information, malicious cyber activities, fraud and 
exploitation, inappropriate use of health data, racism and human 
rights violations within the framework established by international

summary.text: Presents the principle of appropriate use of digital technologies as digital public goods, with protection from misinformation, cyber threats and misuse of health data. It notes the importance of digital determinants of health and lists qualities that appropriate digital health should have, including managing digital waste.

blocks.title: Recognize the urgent need to address the major impediments faced by least-developed countries implementing digital health technologies
blocks.content:
faced by least-developed countries implementing digital 
health technologies 
There is a pressing need to invest in efforts to overcome the major 
impediments that developing countries face in engaging with and 
accessing new digital health technologies, such as an appropriate 
enabling environment, sufficient resources, infrastructure to support 
the digital transformation, education, human capacity, financial 
investment and internet connectivity, as well as issues related to 
legacy infrastructure, technology ownership, privacy, security, and 
adapting and implementing global standards and

summary.text: States the principle that investment is urgently needed to overcome barriers faced by least-developed countries, such as infrastructure, skills, finance, connectivity and standards.

blocks.title: Promote global collaboration and advance the transfer of knowledge on digital health
blocks.content:
knowledge on digital health 
This strategic objective aims to align countries and stakeholders 
to collectively act upon global opportunities to improve health and 
work towards universal health coverage, while meeting challenges, 
identifying and communicating risks, and focusing on threats 
associated with the use of digital technologies both to improve 
health and to enable universal health coverage, the core of the 
health-related Sustainable Development Goals. This objective 
encourages action on common opportunities and challenges 
that are relevant to all countries and stakeholders, reg

summary.text: Introduces strategic objective 1 on global collaboration and knowledge transfer, aiming to align countries and stakeholders on shared opportunities and risks. It covers maximizing partnerships and assessing new health technologies with norms and standards.

summary.text: Introduces the four strategic objectives and lists policy options for objective 1, such as co-creating the strategy and knowledge management. It begins the expected outputs, including governance mechanisms and regular multistakeholder groups.

blocks.title: Advance the implementation of national digital health strategies
blocks.content:
strategies 
Strategic objective 2 aims to stimulate and support every country 
to own, adapt and strengthen its strategy on digital health in a way 
that best suits its vision, national context, health situation and trends, 
available resources and core values.
Strategic objective 2 encourages the development of a national 
strategy on digital health through an all- inclusive multistakeholder 
approach including actors collaborating within communities of 
practice and with consideration to the following core components: 
(1) leadership and governance; (2) investment and operations; 
(3) servic

summary.text: Describes strategic objective 2 on helping each country own and strengthen a national digital health strategy, with core components from leadership and investment to standards and interoperability. It lists policy options such as stakeholder engagement, a national roadmap, open data standards and legal and ethical frameworks for patient safety and data security.

blocks.title: Strengthen governance for digital health at global, regional and national levels
blocks.content:
national levels 
This strategic objective focuses on strengthening the governance 
of digital health at national and international levels through the 
creation of sustainable and robust governance structures and 
building the capacity for digital health at global and national levels. 
Governance for digital health aims to strengthen the capabilities and 
skills needed for countries to promote, innovate and scale up digital 
health technologies.
The strategic objective promotes standards for safety, security, 
privacy, interoperability, and the ethical use of data within and 
outside the health

summary.text: Describes strategic objective 3 on strengthening digital health governance and capacity, with standards for security, privacy, interoperability and ethical data use and a research agenda. It lists policy options and outputs such as a health data regulatory framework and voluntary interoperability guidance. It ends with guidance on digital hospitals and recommendations on pseudonymizing and anonymizing health data.

blocks.title: Advocate people-centred health systems that are enabled by digital health
blocks.content:
digital health 
This strategic objective advances digital health literacy, gender 
equality and women’s empowerment and inclusive approaches to 
adoption and management of digital health technologies.
The strategic objective places people at the centre of digital health 
through the adoption and use of digital health technologies in 
scaling up and strengthening health service delivery. The individual 
is an essential component in the delivery of trust-based, people-
centred care. This focus covers not only patients, families and 
communities but also the health workers who need to be prepared

summary.text: Describes strategic objective 4 on people-centred health systems enabled by digital health, covering digital literacy, gender equality and readiness of health workers. It lists policy options on population health management, public participation and training. Outputs include global minimum health data standards and guidance on personalized medicine.

blocks.title: Commit
blocks.content:
Encourage countries and stakeholders to commit themselves to the 
implementation of the global strategy on digital health. In order to 
reach the strategic objectives of the global strategy, the Secretariat, 
Member States and stakeholders shall maintain their voluntary 
commitment and contributions, respecting national priorities, 
capabilities and resources.

summary.text: Describes the commit component of the framework for action, asking countries and stakeholders to make voluntary commitments to implement the strategy.

blocks.title: Catalyse
blocks.content:
Generate and sustain a conducive environment to create, scale up 
and maintain processes that will facilitate collaboration towards 
implementing the global strategy. This component envisages the 
generation of a cooperative environment that is conducive to 
the creation, introduction and scaling up of appropriate digital 
health technologies and enabling processes that will facilitate and 
accelerate the implementation of the global strategy and 
its objectives.
The Secretariat will promote collaboration among stakeholders 
to ensure progress by building synergies, facilitating technical

summary.text: Describes the catalyse component, creating a cooperative environment for scaling up digital health technologies, with the Secretariat promoting collaboration.

blocks.title: FRAMEWORK FOR ACTION
blocks.content:
The framework for action aims to facilitate the implementation of the 
global strategy by providing a structure and tools for collaboration. 
Working collectively towards shared strategic objectives, local and global 
partners can accommodate diversity and jointly consider concepts, road 
maps, methods, tools, funding and other factors to help implementation 
and support countries in various development contexts to make optimal 
use of digital health technologies.
	
FRAMEWORK FOR ACTION
The framework for action is guided by four major components: commit, 
catalyse, measure, and enhance and ite

summary.text: Explains that the framework for action provides structure and tools for collaboration, guided by four components and accompanied by an action plan for each strategic objective.

blocks.title: Measure
blocks.content:
Create and adopt processes and metrics for monitoring and 
evaluating the effectiveness of the global strategy. This component 
calls for the continuous assessment of whether the global strategy 
on digital health has been true to its purpose and effective in 
supporting countries.
The Secretariat will measure the effectiveness of the global strategy 
from data collected globally and will report findings to 
Member States.

summary.text: Describes the measure component, under which the Secretariat will assess the strategy's effectiveness from global data and report to Member States.

blocks.title: Enhance and iterate
blocks.content:
Undertake a new cycle of actions based on what has been 
experienced, measured and learned. This component will respond to 
feedback on the progress of global strategy in adapting to emerging 
digital health technologies. The action plan will be reviewed annually 
to determine whether a new cycle of new actions is needed to deliver 
on the strategic objectives.
The Secretariat and its partners will propose, exercise and 
continuously refine the global strategy as well as its iterative 
assessment and decision-making processes.
	
FRAMEWORK FOR ACTION
collaboration, and developing digital global

summary.text: Describes the enhance and iterate component, with annual review of the action plan to decide on new cycles of action. It also notes collaboration on quality-assured digital global public goods.

blocks.content: Figure 1, a colour-coded framework summarizing implementation of the action plan, with columns Objectives, Outcomes, Outputs, Policy & Action and Target impacts. Each strategic objective forms a row: SO1 Collaboration and knowledge transfer → global alignment to address opportunities and challenges → increasingly appropriate and sustainable digital health ecosystem; SO2 Digital strategy implementation → strategic vision and integrated action at the national level → cost-effective and efficient health systems and services; SO3 Digital health governance → actions and investments based on informed decisions → accelerated digitalization of the health and well-being sector; SO4 Human-centred health systems → people empowered to make healthy and health-enabling choices → healthier populations. Each row also lists three outputs and four policy and action areas.

blocks.title: IMPLEMENTATION OF THE STRATEGY AND ACTION PLAN
blocks.content:
AND ACTION PLAN
The global strategy on digital health aims to support and respond 
to the growing needs of countries to implement appropriate digital 
technologies in accordance with their health priorities and to make 
progress towards universal health coverage and the health-related 
Sustainable Development Goals. It also responds to the objectives of 
WHO’s Thirteenth General Programme of Work, 2019–2023. 
Figure 1 below summarizes the action plan.
Fig. 1. Summary implementation of the action plan

summary.text: Introduces implementation of the strategy and action plan in line with country health priorities, universal health coverage and WHO's Thirteenth General Programme of Work, with a summary figure.

blocks.title: General implementation principles
blocks.content:
implementation 
principles
The Secretariat will work closely with Member States, other bodies 
in the United Nations system, international partners and other 
stakeholders to implement the global strategy. It is intended that 
various stakeholders will take the strategic objectives forward at 
national, regional and global levels. These stakeholders mainly 
include, but are not limited to, intergovernmental and international 
organizations; non-State actors such as nongovernmental and civil 
society organizations, donors and aid agencies, foundations and 
development banks; universities and re

summary.text: Sets out general principles for implementing the strategy with Member States and many stakeholders, with timelines, milestones and core process indicators. It discusses financing needs and stresses that countries should choose actions suited to their digital health maturity. It notes that the annex describes short-, medium- and long-term actions and that progress will be reported to the Assembly.

blocks.title: Specific implementation principles
blocks.content:
implementation
principles
A national interoperable digital health ecosystem should be set up 
in such a way that the information technology health infrastructures 
are both interoperable among each other and, allowing for 
	
differences in national legislation and policies, capable of sharing 
health data with infrastructures of other countries.
The information technology health infrastructure to be applied within 
an interoperable digital health ecosystem will be based on commonly 
agreed use cases in the public health-care sector, its functional 
requirements and a set of functional and tech

summary.text: Sets out specific principles for a national interoperable digital health ecosystem based on agreed use cases, standards and a sound legal framework. It covers protecting health data, digital identification and a coordinated approach to the economics of health data.

blocks.title: MONITORING AND EVALUATION
blocks.content:
The action plan calls for Member States and the Secretariat to 
dynamically monitor the maturity level of digital health in countries 
and institutions and to assess the implementation of digital health 
strategies through standard agreed-upon metrics. These measures 
should include both the status and performance of digital health 
interventions and include established monitoring and evaluation 
models to facilitate monitoring of the contribution of digital health to 
health system processes, health workforce processes and individual 
health needs.
Steps will be taken to implement a value mea

summary.text: Describes monitoring and evaluation through standard metrics on digital health maturity and a value measurement model, while minimizing extra data burdens. Based on the shown end, the block also begins the glossary with definitions such as digital divide and digital health.
